title: An autoscaling simulator that failed its own test
question: Which [autoscaling](p1:serverless) signal, queue depth (requests waiting per replica), requests in flight per replica or GPU utilisation, gives the best cost and p99 trade-off in a traffic spike? Does a faster [cold start](p1:coldstart) change the answer? The simulator built to answer it failed its own [validation gate](p2:gate) twice.

requirements.text: Cold-start lag, latency under load and GPU utilisation come from hardware; only the autoscaler's control loop is simulated.
requirements.why: The gate then tests exactly the modelled part. Assuming how utilisation maps to load would invent the effect under test.

requirements.text: Judge each signal by every cost/p99 trade-off its threshold grid reaches, not by one tuning.
requirements.why: Every policy has thresholds, and whichever set you publish decides the winner.

requirements.short: Vary only the cold start: A vs C
requirements.text: Arm A (nothing cached, median 81.07 s) and arm C (fully cached, 39.37 s) differ only in cold-start lag; spike and traffic stay fixed.
requirements.why: H3 asks whether a faster cold start shrinks the gap between signals; anything else moving with the arm would confound it. (The A1 unit's 81.12 s also counts arm A's one image-pull run.)

requirements.short: No answer before the model passes
requirements.text: The simulator must reproduce a real replica's latency under a test fixed in advance; if it fails, publish the failure, not the answer.
requirements.why: Tuning a simulator until it agrees is "fabrication with extra steps" (the design spec); [a failed gate is a result](p2:failed).

requirements.text: Hypotheses, grids, control parameters, the traffic rule and the pass rule are committed before the sweep or validation they govern, except H1, H2 and H4, which were defined after the frontiers were seen; later changes are dated [amendments](p2:amendment) saying what had been seen.
requirements.why: Otherwise the traffic could be tuned until a signal wins, or the tolerance until the model passes.

requirements.text: Build and test the simulator, sweep and gate arithmetic with no GPU; keep paid runs small and stoppable; re-derive every number on a laptop.
requirements.why: Most of it was buildable offline. Estimate $35–60; billed $6.07, partly because the closed-loop run never happened.
requirements.unlinked_reason: Met by process: "Build the simulator with no GPU" and "Commit the pass rule" come before any paid run, and one script re-derives every published number from committed files.

concepts.plain: One replica's latency, throughput and GPU utilisation at fixed numbers of requests in flight, 1 to 128, three runs each; 256 ran out of GPU memory. The simulator reads service times from it instead of modelling [continuous batching](p1:batching).
**In flight = arrival rate × time each request spends.** At 128 in flight and 0.606 s each, one replica completes 128 / 0.606 = 211.2 req/s: the "saturation" every traffic rate here is a fraction of.

concepts.term: Why GPU utilisation is blind here
concepts.plain: nvidia-smi reads 1.0 from one request upward and 0 only when idle. A utilisation autoscaler sees "fully busy" whenever a replica serves anything, so it adds replicas at every chance up to its cap: busy and drowning look the same.

concepts.term: Frontier, dominance and the iso-cost slice
concepts.plain: A **policy** is a signal plus its up and down thresholds; over 30 simulated spikes it gives a median cost (**replica-seconds**, billed from each launch) and a median per-run p99. It is **dominated** if another costs no more, has no worse p99 and is better on one; the rest are the **frontier**. The **iso-cost budget** is the cheapest spend at which every signal has a policy; the **gap** is the worst signal's p99 there minus the best's. H3: the gap at least halves from arm A to arm C, on step and ramp.

Per 10 s bin, each real repeat's residual is its p50 minus its own prediction. A bin **misses** when all three residuals sit on one side by more than 1 ms. With no bias each repeat is a coin flip, so a perfect model misses at most 2 × (1/2)³ = 1/4 of bins. **Pass:** at least 10 judged bins, at most half missing.

Rented GPUs of one model are not equally fast, and RunPod picks the host. Every other host measured had 4 to 18% lower latency than the curve's, more at high load: about the size of the gate's misses (14% and 13%). A measured cause, not shown to be the whole one.

walkthrough.title: One spike through the queue-depth control loop
walkthrough.lead: One replayed run: queue-depth policy (up 4, down 1), arm C step spike, repetition 0 of the committed sweep. Simulated by a model that failed its gate twice, not measured.

steps.say: Spike: 253.4 req/s from t = 0 to 190 s, but one replica completes about 211.2 ([Little's Law](a2:littles)). Every 5 s the controller reads waiting requests per serving replica: up at 4 or more, down at 1 or less.
t = 5: the queue is 196 per replica, so UP one replica, billed from launch. It serves after a [cold start](p1:coldstart) drawn from arm C's runs (median 39.37 s); this draw is 39.4 s.
t = 10 to 30: the queue grows (374 at t = 10), but one 30 s cooldown after any action, up or down, holds the fleet. At t = 35 it is 1,416 and replica 2 is still starting: UP again, replica 3.
t = 44.4 (5 + 39.4): replica 2 starts serving. Two replicas complete up to 2 × 211.2 = 422.4 req/s against 253.4 arriving, so the backlog drains.
t = 65: queue 0 (requests wait only once all 128 slots per replica are full), so DOWN. The newest replica goes first: replica 3, still starting, billed for 30 s and never served.
t = 95: queue still 0, cooldown over: DOWN to one replica, with the spike still on at 253.4 req/s. A queue of 0 means enough capacity, and this rule removes the replica that made it enough.
The backlog rebuilds: t = 125, queue 1,274, UP; t = 155, queue 2,546, UP. The first serves at about 164 s, some 69 s after the scale-down: a second cold start under overload.
t = 185: queue 0, so DOWN removes replica 5, still starting. t = 215, spike over (it ended at 190 s): queue 0, DOWN to one replica.

Cost: 400 for replica 1 plus 90 + 30 + 90 + 30 = 240 for the four launched: 640 replica-seconds; p99 11.73 s. Of 19 × 30 = 570 replayed queue-depth runs, 410 make these exact moves; all scale down before 190 s.

walkthrough.takeaway: In this simulator a queue of 0 means enough capacity, so queue depth scales down mid-spike and pays a second cold start: cheap at 640, slower at 11.15 s against 7.20 s. Real autoscalers were not tested.

decisions.title: Answer in a simulator, held to a gate
decisions.problem: The question needs dozens of policies run thirty times each through real spikes: out of budget on rented GPUs.
options: Run the policies live on real replicas
A model of vLLM's scheduler in place of the measured curve
A simulator trusted without a test
A simulator fed only measured inputs, gated first
decisions.chosen: A simulator fed only measured inputs, gated first
decisions.why: Modelling the scheduler would replace a measurement with an assumption about what [continuous batching](p1:batching) does to latency; the curve measures it, and only the control loop is code. Discrete events need no tick size, and a seed makes runs reproducible. A new replica is absent until a lag resampled from artifact 1's runs, then fully serving.
decisions.cost: If the gate fails there is no answer, and it failed twice. The design's second gate, one real closed-loop autoscaling run, was never built.
decisions.why_short: Live tests cost too much and modelling the scheduler would assume what the curve measures, so measured inputs feed a gated simulator.
decisions.cost_short: No answer if the gate fails; it failed twice.

serves.because: Lags, latency and utilisation are measured; only the control loop is code, and that is what the gate tests.
The simulator's answer counts only once it passes a pre-registered test.

uses.because: The engine enters as this measured curve, not a queueing formula.

decisions.title: One controller, a grid per signal, frontiers
decisions.problem: Any published tuning decides the winner, and the signals do not share units: utilisation is a fraction, the others are counts.
options: Hand-pick each signal's best thresholds
One shared grid, 2 to 16, for all three
One controller, a grid per signal in its own units; compare frontiers
decisions.chosen: One controller, a grid per signal in its own units; compare frontiers
decisions.why: A shared 2 to 16 grid puts every threshold above utilisation's maximum of 1, so it never scales and H2 "wins" by a units mismatch (checked: 0 scale-ups at 2.0). Fixed for every policy: a 30 s cooldown (one pause after any action, up or down), a 5 s evaluation, a 12-replica cap, 30 repetitions.
decisions.cost: Grids were fixed on 2026-09-05 against a placeholder curve that stopped at 64 in flight, and not revisited. On the measured curve each signal's step frontier is one point, and the iso-cost budget, 3,095 replica-seconds, is utilisation's floor: it never constrains the other two.
decisions.why_short: Published thresholds decide the winner, so each signal is swept over a grid in its own units.
decisions.cost_short: Grids fixed on a placeholder curve; on the measured one each frontier is a point and the budget never binds.

serves.because: Every threshold pair is run, so no single tuning picks the winner.

uses.because: Signals are compared frontier against frontier, at the iso-cost budget.
Utilisation gets a 0 to 1 grid, yet reads 1.0 above all of it, so its 19 policies ran at the cap.

decisions.title: Tolerance from reality's own repeatability
decisions.problem: How close must the simulator be? The bar has to be fixed before any real run.
options: A chosen tolerance, say 5%
Compare against a fresh random draw of the traffic
Require every bin inside the real runs' band
Leave the number of repeats open
Three repeats of the exact trace; at most half the 10 s bins may miss
decisions.chosen: Three repeats of the exact trace; at most half the 10 s bins may miss
decisions.why: A model cannot be required to be more reproducible than the system it models, so three real repeats set the tolerance, on the exact trace so traffic randomness cannot pose as model error. A perfect model still misses up to a quarter of bins, so "every bin" would often fail it; a model biased beyond the system's own spread misses most bins (the pre-registration's example, three bins in four, fails 92% of the time at 10 bins). Exactly three repeats: a min–max range only widens with more.
decisions.cost: Correlated bins make a perfect model fail more often than the stated 2% at 10 bins (2.5% simulated, near 5% with host effects). p50 suited bins of a few hundred requests; the replay's held over a thousand. Two attempts at most.
decisions.why_short: A model cannot be more reproducible than the system, so three real repeats set the tolerance.
decisions.cost_short: Correlated bins make a perfect model fail more often than stated; two attempts at most.

serves.because: It is the test the answer must pass: a perfect model passes it, a biased one fails.
Committed on 2026-10-03, before any real validation run.

uses.because: The miss rule is the tolerance: all three repeats on one side is a miss.

decisions.title: Choose the traffic by a ranking-blind rule
decisions.problem: As registered, the spike peaked at 3.4× one replica's capacity and all 55 policies gave the same p99 to nine decimals. Later, on the measured curve, the replacement starved queue depth.
options: Keep the registered traffic and report the tie
Raise the replica cap
Widen the threshold grids upward
Search by a measure that cannot prefer a signal
decisions.chosen: Search by a measure that cannot prefer a signal
decisions.why: Past every threshold from the first evaluation, every signal says "scale up" at once, and with an 81 s cold start no replica arrives in time, so only cost differs. A bigger cap never binds; wider grids would redefine each signal's range. A count of distinct outcomes cannot pick a winner, and the first re-choice refuted the hypotheses, which a rigged choice would not.
decisions.cost: Choosing traffic after seeing data is a real hazard: per-policy p99s had been printed before the second search's criteria were written, as the amendment says. The gate stayed at 0.95× capacity while the sweep moved to 1.20×.
decisions.why_short: As registered, all 55 policies gave one p99; counting distinct outcomes cannot prefer a signal.
decisions.cost_short: Choosing traffic after seeing data is a disclosed hazard; the gate never tested the sweep's overload.

serves.because: Rates and the 190 s length are the same for both arms, so the arms differ only in lag.
Each re-choice is a dated amendment; the second search's criteria were committed before its code.

uses.because: Baseline and peak are fractions of one replica's Little's-law saturation.
A spike past every threshold gives every policy one p99, so no frontier separates the signals.

decisions.title: Validate the engine, not the platform
decisions.problem: The replica sits behind RunPod's load balancer, which, the probes found, caps, routes, stalls and drops requests in ways the simulator does not model.
options: RunPod's queue API (/run) for the replay
Two pinned replicas, as first signed
Judge client latency, or bin by send time
Retry failures until they succeed
One replica, judged on what its engine received; an unanswered 502 retried once
decisions.chosen: One replica, judged on what its engine received; an unanswered 502 retried once
decisions.why: The queue API allows 1,000 requests per 10 s, far below the replay's planned peak of about 400 req/s. The load balancer fills one worker before the next, so two replicas would score its routing against the simulator's even split; it holds and releases bursts, so send times would score its stalls as model misses. Retrying until success hides failures.
decisions.cost: The prediction can no longer be written before the run, and the bursts become model input: the engine held more than its 128 running cap, up to 512 counting requests queued inside it. Even splitting across replicas stays untested.
decisions.why_short: The load balancer fills one worker first and stalls, so the gate judges what the engine received.
decisions.cost_short: No prediction before the run; even splitting across replicas never tested.

serves.because: The gate stays a test of the engine model, not of a platform the model never described.
Server latency is what the curve measured; client latency adds network and load-balancer time.

uses.because: Each repeat is held to its own prediction, so bursts that differ per repeat still compare like with like.
Capped at 128 running, the curve's top level, the engine queued the rest, as the simulator does.

decisions.title: One disclosed fix, then publish the failure
decisions.problem: Attempt one failed; an exploratory re-measurement pointed to host speed. What may change without bending the test?
options: Keep adjusting until it passes
Fit the curve to the validation runs
Publish the frontiers with a caveat
One disclosed fix, declared the last attempt; then publish the failure
decisions.chosen: One disclosed fix, declared the last attempt; then publish the failure
decisions.why: Tuning until it agrees is what R4 forbids. The fix was two numbers per repeat, latency ratios at 64 and 128 in flight measured on the same worker before its replay, on traffic the gate never judges. It failed the other way by about as much (the engine 14% faster than predicted, then 13% slower).
decisions.cost: No measured answer. Why the calibration over-corrected is an untested hypothesis (closed-loop calibration, open-loop bursty replay; one host). H1, H2 and H4 were defined only after the frontiers were seen, and are labelled so.
decisions.why_short: Tuning until it agrees is fabrication: one disclosed fix, declared the last, then the failure is the result.
decisions.cost_short: No measured answer; the over-correction is unexplained; H1, H2, H4 were defined after seeing frontiers.

serves.because: After the second failure the failure was published, not the frontiers.
The fix was a signed amendment, declared the last attempt, before it ran.

uses.because: The fix measured each repeat's host speed, the cause attempt one pointed to.
Both failures read the same way: all three repeats on one side, almost every bin.

flow.label: Specify a gated simulator, then re-base on artifact 1
flow.detail: The August spec: three signals, two spike shapes, a gate. On 09-04 the final spec took artifact 1's numbers, and the pre-registration followed that night, before simulator code.
flow.output: design spec, final spec and pre-registration, before simulator code

flow.label: Build the simulator with no GPU
flow.detail: Lag resampling, event queue, one controller, sweep and frontiers, on a placeholder curve flagged unmeasured. A discard rule that dropped every run was amended before any result.
flow.output: autoscale/: simulator, controller, sweep and frontiers, tested offline

flow.label: Find the traffic made the question unanswerable
flow.detail: After a fix (the three signals had been scored on three different traces), all 55 policies gave the same p99. A ranking-blind probe chose new traffic; medians and intervals replaced means.

flow.label: Commit the pass rule before any real run
flow.detail: The gate's arithmetic, in a module with no path to artifact 1's code, then the pass rule: three repeats, 10 s bins, at most half missing.
flow.output: validation_band.py and the pass rule in experiment-a2.md

flow.label: Measure the curve; re-choose traffic, criteria first
flow.detail: The curve, 1 to 128 in flight (256 ran out of memory); recon: pinning holds capacity, a driven scale-up is a real cold start. The old traffic starved queue depth; search criteria were committed, then the search run.

flow.label: Probe the load balancer; amend the gate three times
flow.detail: At RunPod's default scaler value 4 the first probe delivered about 17 req/s; later probes found fill-first routing, stalls and unanswered 502s. Amendments: retry such a 502 once; one replica; judge engine arrivals.
flow.output: five probes; three amendments; three early repeats kept unjudged

flow.label: Attempt one fails; host speed implicated
flow.detail: 34 of 37 judged bins missed, the engine faster than predicted. One void repeat (a worker restarted on the old image) was re-run. A re-measurement afterwards ruled out the engine flag and found hosts differ by about the size of the miss. Host speed is a measured cause, not shown to be the whole one: attempt one's own host had about 7% lower latency at ~100 in flight, while the quiet bins missed by 14%.

flow.label: Calibrate the host; attempt two fails
flow.detail: Signed as the second and last attempt. 37 of 37 bins missed the other way, the engine slower than the calibrated prediction.

flow.label: Publish the failure; label the simulator
flow.detail: An exploratory speed check; H1, H2, H4 defined after the frontiers were seen; one analysis file feeds every number; the post leads with both failures; a probability claim corrected on 10-18.

results.title: The service curve: latency as load rises

chart.x_label: requests in flight on one replica
chart.note: Whiskers: lowest and highest of the three runs. At 256 in flight the engine died (out of GPU memory) in 3 of 3 runs, so the curve stops at 128.

results.axis: Measured: one replica of vLLM serving Qwen3-8B on an RTX 4090, median end-to-end latency at each fixed number of requests in flight.
results.read_as: Latency only doubles from 1 to 128 in flight while throughput grows about 58-fold: what [continuous batching](p1:batching) buys. The simulator reads every service time from this one host's curve.
results.takeaway: One replica holds 128 times the requests in flight for twice the latency: the danger is the queue past 128, not slow requests.
results.arithmetic: Each point is the median of three runs' medians; 0.606 / 0.284 = 2.1.

results.title: Throughput, and the traffic set from it

chart.x_label: requests in flight on one replica
chart.note: GPU utilisation (nvidia-smi) read 1.0 at every level from 1 to 128, and 0 when idle, so it is not drawn: it would be a flat line at the top.

results.axis: Measured: requests one replica completes per second at each fixed number in flight. Dashed: traffic levels set from it, as multiples of saturation (211.2 req/s).
results.read_as: The validation replay peaked at 0.95× saturation (200.6 req/s), which is 0.98× of the 204.4 measured at 128 in flight; the sweep's spike peaked at 1.20× saturation (253.4 req/s) and stayed there, a regime the gate never tested.
results.takeaway: Every rate is a fraction of one replica's capacity: the gate checked the model below it, the sweep ran above it.
results.arithmetic: Saturation by Little's Law: 128 / 0.606 s = 211.2 req/s (measured at 128: 204.4). Baseline 0.70 × 211.2 = 147.8; peaks add 0.25 or 0.5 × 211.2: 200.6 and 253.4 req/s. 200.6 / 204.4 = 0.98 of measured throughput.

results.title: The test, twice: which side the engine landed on

chart.x_label: engine arrival time, start of each 10 s bin (s)
chart.note: Attempt one's bins at 40, 230 and 270 s did not miss.

results.axis: Per judged 10 s bin: real p50 ÷ predicted p50 per repeat, median of three, minus 1. Real: measured on RunPod. Predicted: the simulator fed the arrivals that engine received.
results.read_as: Below zero, the engine was faster than predicted. Attempt one is below in every bin, down to −89% after load-balancer bursts; attempt two, calibrated to its host, is 12–16% above in every bin.
results.takeaway: Uncalibrated, the model predicted latency too high (engine 14% faster; 34 of 37 bins miss); calibrated, too low (13% slower; 37 of 37). The size held: about what a host changes.
results.arithmetic: Median over the 37 judged bins: 0.856 (14% below) and 1.127 (13% above); per bin, 0.11 to 0.955 and 1.116 to 1.16. Recomputed from the repeat records.

results.title: Host speed: one GPU model, different latency
results.short: Hosts differ as much as the miss

chart.left_label: lower latency than the curve's host

results.axis: Measured: server latency on each RunPod host relative to the curve's host (ozhetwnhompob9), at high load. Bars: lowest to highest of three runs; ku80i8usxw3st5 has one reading.
results.read_as: Every other host measured had 7 to 18% lower latency than the curve's at high load: the size of the gate's misses. RunPod picks the host; the simulator knows one. Three hosts show a spread, not a distribution.
results.takeaway: Hosts differ by about the size of the miss, and a one-host curve cannot predict which one RunPod picks: part of the miss, not shown to be all of it.

results.title: The load balancer's default cap: offered against delivered
results.short: A default capped two GPUs at 17/s

chart.note: Probe 1 stopped after 100 req/s: the driver could not start another thread.

results.axis: Measured on 2026-10-05: two RTX 4090 workers behind RunPod's load-balancing endpoint, 30 s per offered rate. Exploratory probes, not pre-registered.
results.read_as: At RunPod's default scaler value of 4 the path delivered about 17 req/s whatever was offered, while the engine's p50 stayed at 0.31 s: requests waited in the load balancer, which caps each worker at that many in flight.
results.takeaway: A setting RunPod documents only for autoscaling capped two GPUs at 17 req/s: $36.02 against $2.05 per million requests.
results.arithmetic: At the billed $1.1085/h ($1.11 rounded) for 2 workers: $36.02 per million at 17.1 req/s, $2.05 at 300.7; 300.7 / 17.1 = 17.6, the post's 18×.

results.title: UNVALIDATED: what each policy spent and reached (arm C, step)

frontier.name: best p99 at each cost, any signal

chart.note: SIMULATED, FAILED VALIDATION. The p99 axis starts near 7 s. Each signal's own frontier is one point: its cheapest policy is also its fastest. Pairs whose down threshold is not below the up threshold are skipped (3 of 20 for in flight, 1 for each other signal), hence 17, 19 and 19 policies.

results.axis: Simulated, not measured, by a model that failed its gate twice. Each dot is one policy (signal and thresholds): its median over 30 simulated step spikes with arm C's cold starts.
results.read_as: All 19 queue-depth policies spent 640 replica-seconds and all 19 utilisation policies sat at the cap, 3,095; within each, only p99 differs. The budget line constrains no one, so H3's 3.96 s "gap" is queue depth spending 640 against 2,320–3,095. Queue depth is cheap because it scales down once the backlog clears (see the walkthrough); a rerun with scale-down off (exploratory, not committed) brought its p99 close to the others', so the gap mostly reflects the scale-down rule.
results.takeaway: Even as the simulator's answer, the comparison is mostly one of spend: the budget never binds and each frontier is one point.
results.arithmetic: Gap = worst reached p99 − best at the budget: 11.15 − 7.20 = 3.95 s on rounded values (post: 3.96, 95% interval 3.52–4.56). Arm A's step: 0.082 s, so H3's halving fails.

interview.pitch30: I tried to find which autoscaling signal, queue depth, requests in flight or GPU utilisation, gives the best cost and tail-latency trade-off for an LLM server whose new replicas take tens of seconds to over a minute to start. Live tests were too expensive, so I built a simulator from measured inputs with a pre-registered test it had to pass. It failed twice: it first predicted latency too high, which I traced partly to host speed, then, calibrated to the host, too low, for a reason I could not settle. So I published the failure, and two measured findings: GPU utilisation reads 100% from one request, and RunPod's load balancer caps each worker at 4 requests in flight by default.
interview.pitch120: A new LLM replica takes a median 39 to 81 seconds to start, so the signal an autoscaler watches has to see trouble early. I compared queue depth, requests in flight and GPU utilisation by their whole cost-versus-p99 frontiers, and asked whether a faster cold start shrinks the difference. Dozens of policies run thirty times each was out of budget on real GPUs, so I built a simulator where every input is measured and only the control loop is code, and committed a pass rule before any real run: replay a real spike three times; a 10-second bin misses if all three runs land on one side of the prediction; more than half missing fails. It failed with the engine 14% faster than predicted. A re-measurement ruled out the engine flag and showed hosts differ by about that much, so host speed is part of the cause. I made one disclosed fix, declared it the last attempt, and it failed 13% the other way. So I published the failure instead of the frontiers. Two findings are measured: nvidia-smi utilisation reads 1.0 from one request, and RunPod's load balancer caps requests per worker at a setting documented only for autoscaling, which made each request 18 times dearer. The paid part cost $6.07.

followups.q: So which signal should I use?
followups.a: Not answered by measurement. Measured: nvidia-smi utilisation reads 1.0 from one request up, so all 19 simulated utilisation policies ran to the cap. The unvalidated simulator puts the three within 82 ms on arm A's step, queue depth spending 880 replica-seconds against 2,535–3,095. Practically, on this stack: don't scale on nvidia-smi utilisation; check the load balancer first.

followups.q: Why trust a simulator at all?
followups.a: By default I didn't. 55 policies × 30 repetitions × 4 sweeps is 6,600 simulated spikes, unaffordable live, so it had to pass a rule committed on 2026-10-03, before any real run. It failed, and that is what I published.

followups.q: Wasn't the calibration just moving the goalposts?
followups.a: One disclosed fix was allowed, and the amendment declared it the last attempt before it ran: two numbers per repeat, from traffic the gate never judges. It failed the other way by about as much, which is the finding: the host moves latency as much as the model's error.

followups.q: You changed the traffic twice after seeing data. Isn't that p-hacking?
followups.a: The registered spike gave every policy one p99: no question to answer. Both re-choices used measures that cannot prefer a signal, and the second search's criteria were committed before its code. I concede that per-policy p99s had been seen (the amendment says so), and the gate never tested the overload the sweep ran in.

followups.q: What would a careful reviewer flag in your own write-up?
followups.a: The gap's interval is called paired, but the code pairs only queue depth with in-flight at shared thresholds; utilisation runs on other traces. H3's wording says "p99-damage spread", the spec's integral over an SLO, but the analysis uses each run's p99 and no SLO exists. And the post omits the request shape (random 13-token prompts, 16 output tokens) and the absent-or-serving replica model.

Measure host speed per run from the start; settle the load balancer before the gate; validate in the sweep's overload; build the closed-loop gate. And revisit the grids: in-flight's tops out at 16, while one replica holds over 64 in flight at baseline alone (139.5 req/s at 64, under the 147.8 baseline). My untested reading: every in-flight threshold is crossed at once, so its grid only sets where scaling stops; up-2 and up-4 hit the cap.

interview.limits: No measured answer: every frontier, H1–H4 verdict, gap and per-signal dollar figure is from a simulator that failed validation twice, and H1, H2, H4 were defined after the frontiers were seen. The control loop was never compared with a real autoscaler. The gate tested 0.95× saturation (0.98× of measured throughput), the sweep ran at 1.20×. Even load splitting is assumed; RunPod fills one worker first. One provider, GPU, model, engine version (vLLM 0.27.1) and request shape; replicas absent or serving; 6 hosts seen, 3 timed. Load-balancer findings: five unregistered probes on 2026-10-05.

recall.q: Which requirement breaks if the frontiers are published although the gate failed?
recall.a: R4, no answer before the model passes: every number would be an unvalidated model's, presented as a finding.

recall.q: Why does a perfect model still miss about one bin in four, and how does the pass rule allow for it?
recall.a: Unbiased, each repeat lands above or below its prediction like a coin, so all three on one side has probability at most 2 × 1/8 = 1/4, less with the 1 ms margin. The rule passes with at least 10 judged bins and at most half missing.

recall.q: Attempt one missed with the engine faster, attempt two, calibrated, with it slower. What does the pair let you conclude?
recall.a: The model's error is about the size of a host's effect (14% against 13%), so a one-host curve cannot predict the hosts RunPod picks. Host speed is a measured cause, not shown to be the whole one, and the pair does not say which way a given host goes.

recall.q: Why do two failures mean the answer is not in this study, rather than "try a third fix"?
recall.a: The calibration was signed as the second and last attempt before it ran; a third fix after two failures is the tuning-until-it-agrees R4 forbids.

recall.q: Why does the gate judge the arrivals the engine received, not the driver's send times?
recall.a: RunPod's load balancer held requests and released bursts, so the engine never received the schedule. Judged by send time, the platform's stalls would count as simulator misses.

recall.q: Why is GPU utilisation blind on this engine, and what did it do to its policies?
recall.a: nvidia-smi reads 1.0 from one request up, above every threshold (highest 0.95), so it scales up at every chance: all 19 policies ran at the 12-replica cap.

recall.q: As registered, all 55 policies gave the same p99. Why, and why not just raise the replica cap?
recall.a: At 3.4× capacity every signal is past every threshold from the first evaluation and no replica arrives within the 81 s cold start, so all act alike. The cap never bound: 12, 24 and 64 gave identical results.

recall.q: On arm C the simulated gap is 3.96 s. Why is that not a clean signal effect?
recall.a: The budget, utilisation's floor (3,095), never constrains the other two, so the gap compares queue depth at 640 replica-seconds with signals spending 2,320–3,095.

recall.q: Which requirement does holding the spike fixed across arms protect, and in what unit is the spike set?
recall.a: R3, vary only the cold start. Its rates are fractions of one replica's Little's-law saturation, 211.2 req/s, and its 190 s length is the same for both arms.
